newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal plans to spend $4 billion to reduce poverty.
newsitem.headline: Nepal plans to spend $4 billion to reduce poverty.

text.p: Nepal plans to spend 225.2 billion rupees ($4 billion) over the next five years in developmental projects to reduce poverty in the Himalayan kingdom, government officials said on Sunday.
Currently, 45 percent of Nepal's 21 million people live below the poverty line, or at less than the minimum average calorie consumption needed to survive.

"The objective is to bring down the poverty to 32.5 percent in the ninth plan (1997-2002) and to 10 percent in the 12th plan," Mangal Sinddhi Manandhar, vice-chairman of the National Planning Commission, told a meeting of the National Development Council (NDC) on Sunday.
The NDC is Nepal's highest planning body and is headed by Prime Minister Lokendra Bahadur Chand.
Officials said the two-day meeting was expected to approve the ninth plan due to begin on July 16.
Nepal has been maintaining a Soviet-style planned economy since 1957.
Critics said administration of development projects was slower than expected due to successive changes of government.
"Economic development in the past failed to take a clear cut direction in absence of a long-term vision," Manandhar said.
Nepal has had five different governments since multi-party democracy was established seven years ago.
Officials said the real gross domestic product (GDP), expected to grow by five percent in 1997, would maintain a 7.2 percent annual rate of growth in the next 20 years.
They said the government planned to create 5.27 million additional jobs in the next two decades.
The government also wants to reduce the infant mortality rate to 50 from 79 for every 1,000 live births and raise the literacy rate to 70 percent from 40 percent.
Nepal is one of the world's 10 poorest countries. Officials said foreign aid accounted for 65 percent of the total development cost of the eighth plan ending mid-July 1997.
That figure had been reduced to 57.9 percent or 130.5 billion rupees ($2.3 billion) for the new plan.
"Since a major portion of the budget has to be earmarked for servicing external debt, a policy has been adopted to reduce the ratio of foreign loans," a government official said.
A Finance Ministry report said Nepal's outstanding external debt stood at $2.15 billion in mid-April 1996.
